title: Reference Monitor

validation.research: Five primary sources: Anderson 1972 Volume II section 4.1.1 printed pages 22–23, visually read from scanned PDF pages 30–31; three NIST glossary entries distinguish reference monitor, reference monitor concept and security kernel; official PostgreSQL row-security documentation establishes privileged exceptions. Complete mediation, tamper protection and verifiability are requirements, not properties proven by this Python simulator. Authentication, authorization, exact object/action binding, revocation scope, policy evidence failure, trusted administrators, protected audit and logical versus physical boundary are explicit. Monitor Object is a distinct concurrency pattern. No existing exact canonical article found.

checks: exact six modeled outcomes and policy versions
subject/action/resource separation and default deny
no protected-body retrieval on denied requests
malformed input and unknown operations rejected
immutable result and audit snapshots
revocation on next operation without recalling old data
policy unavailable denies and recovery preserves revocation
policy/metadata/audit faults stop before body retrieval
body errors propagate and lock releases
decision log does not imply operation completion
real event-gated mutex contention orders check/use and revocation
same-process access explicitly demonstrates missing isolation

example_limits: Closed-world behavioral simulator with trusted normalized identities, administrators, immutable string bodies and one process-local mutex. It demonstrates permit/deny and policy transitions, not hostile-code isolation, authentication, tamper protection, durable audit, distributed policy consistency, or a security proof. A negative scope test shows direct Python state access remains possible. PostgreSQL behavior is documented context, not a live database experiment.
